categories.label: Fragmented Multi-Tier Supply Chain Coordination
categories.memo: Covers the organizational complexity of coordinating design, fabrication, transport and assembly across many independent contracted parties, and how communication/information failures propagate risk through the chain.

codes.label: Fragmentation and mistrust between contractor and factory/subcontractor
codes.description: The separation of off-site fabrication and on-site assembly across independent, for-profit entities creates mistrust, conflicting goals, and difficulty managing the supply chain as a whole.

codes.label: Poor/obsolete information sharing between parties
codes.description: Reliance on informal or outdated communication channels (email, messaging apps, hard copies) and untimely conveyance of design/schedule information between designer, contractor and manufacturer is a root cause of coordination failures.

codes.label: Multi-project resource competition at manufacturer level
codes.description: Manufacturers/factories serve multiple clients simultaneously, causing poor coordination of resources across projects that undermines performance on any single contract.

codes.label: Design change propagation through the supply chain
codes.description: Late or client-driven design changes disrupt fabrication cycles, cause rework, schedule delay and cost overrun, and damage trust/reputation among stakeholders.

codes.label: Integrated/vertically-integrated delivery reduces coordination burden
codes.description: Design-Build, IPD, supplier-builder integration or full vertical integration reduce the number of contractual interfaces and improve coordination compared to fragmented Design-Bid-Build arrangements.

codes.label: BIM and digital platforms as coordination enablers
codes.description: BIM, digital twins, blockchain and shared information/Kanban-style platforms are identified as key technological enablers bridging communication gaps between offsite and onsite parties.

categories.label: Just-in-Time Delivery and Schedule Coordination
categories.memo: Addresses the operational challenge of aligning fabrication and delivery schedules with on-site assembly needs, and the contractual mechanisms proposed to manage schedule deviations.

codes.label: Contractual rigidity obstructing JIT coordination
codes.description: Static, fixed-price contracts push both parties to rigidly comply with original schedules rather than seek mutually beneficial rescheduling, converting the contract from a coordination 'pull' mechanism into an inflexible 'push' mechanism.

codes.label: Dynamic compensation/incentive mechanisms for schedule changes
codes.description: Proposed real-time surcharge/incentive schemes (e.g., inverse Kanban, rebate contracts) allocate cost of delivery-date changes to whichever party causes them, replacing static one-sided compensation systems.

codes.label: Risk-averse front-loading of deliveries as a substitute for JIT
codes.description: In practice, contractors often order/deliver components early to hedge against on-site delay risk rather than pursue strict JIT, shifting inventory and financing costs onto suppliers.

codes.label: Optimization vs. intuitive transport/schedule planning
codes.description: Transport and assembly scheduling decisions are typically made intuitively/experientially by contractors rather than via optimization models, leading to unnecessary cost and delay that formal planning tools could reduce.

codes.label: Engineer-to-order components limit delivery flexibility
codes.description: Because prefabricated components are typically engineered/customized for a specific project, they cannot be redirected to other buyers if schedules change, heightening the stakes of delivery coordination failures.

codes.label: Storage and space constraints driving JIT necessity
codes.description: Lack of on-site or yard storage space, particularly in high-density urban contexts, makes JIT delivery planning a practical necessity rather than an optional efficiency measure.

categories.label: Transportation and Logistics Risk
categories.memo: Focuses specifically on the physical movement of modules/components — cost, complexity, regulatory constraints, and cross-border issues — as distinct from scheduling/coordination per se.

codes.label: Transportation cost and complexity as adoption barrier
codes.description: Transporting volumetric modules or prefabricated components is markedly more costly and complex than transporting raw materials, representing a significant share of total project cost and a barrier to wider MMC/MiC adoption.

codes.label: Cross-border/off-shore logistics risk
codes.description: Fabrication occurring overseas or across borders (e.g., Mainland China to Hong Kong, East Asia to project site) introduces customs, traffic and jurisdictional uncertainty not present in single-site conventional construction.

codes.label: Regulatory and physical constraints on module transport
codes.description: Module size, weight, and route/traffic control regulations must be assessed before design finalization, constraining design freedom and requiring early contractual commitment.

codes.label: Subsidy and policy mechanisms to offset logistics cost
codes.description: Government subsidy schemes (bilevel contractor-government decision models, revenue-sharing) are proposed/used to offset high transportation and adoption costs and shape contractor procurement decisions.

categories.label: Third-Party and Construction Logistics Services
categories.memo: Concerns the emergence of formal or informal third-party logistics (TPL) / construction logistics service (CLS) arrangements and their contractual embedding, distinct from direct contractor-supplier delivery relationships.

codes.label: Mandated use of logistics service modules via subcontract
codes.description: Main contractors contractually require subcontractors to use particular logistics service modules (material/waste management), making subcontractors non-voluntary customers excluded from initial co-design.

codes.label: Coordination failures among multiple TPL providers
codes.description: Lack of coherence between different logistics service modules and their providers requires an authoritative actor (main contractor) to coordinate them, adding an extra coordination layer.

codes.label: Vendor/material management partnerships as quasi-contracts
codes.description: Vendors formalize expanded roles (warehousing, inventory control, delivery) through nonbinding partnership agreements that function similarly to contracts but sit outside formal subcontract structures.

codes.label: Temporary project structure undermines logistics relationship continuity
codes.description: Because projects are temporary and logistics providers are re-procured each time, trust and value co-creation processes must restart, limiting the benefit of prior contractual relationships.

categories.label: Risk and Responsibility Allocation in Supply/Delivery Contracts
categories.memo: Covers how risk, cost, and responsibility for delivery variability, quality, and schedule are (or should be) allocated between contracting parties, including power asymmetries.

codes.label: Upstream risk transfer to suppliers/subcontractors
codes.description: Construction supply chains show a tendency to push value/supply chain risk upstream onto subcontractors and suppliers, damaging trust and commitment; suppliers bear most risk while builders act mainly as purchasers.

codes.label: Power asymmetry between Tier One builders/developers and suppliers/contractors
codes.description: Dominant parties (large builders, developers) impose onerous contract terms with little negotiating power left to suppliers or contractors, who bear disproportionate cost and schedule risk.

codes.label: Financial risk-management clauses (guarantees, dual-sourcing)
codes.description: Contractual tools such as bank guarantees, insurance certificates, joint trading accounts, and dual/multi-sourcing of identical work are used by builders to manage cash flow and non-performance risk from suppliers.

codes.label: Insufficient design information as a source of contractual risk
codes.description: Incomplete or untimely design information before prefabrication start exposes builders to unforeseen costs, delay, defects and hostile renegotiation.

codes.label: Savings/benefit capture inequities along the subcontracting chain
codes.description: Cost savings generated by off-site prefabrication are passed up the contracting chain to head contractors rather than retained by subcontractors, undermining incentives to collaborate.

codes.label: Revenue/subsidy-sharing contracts for supply chain coordination
codes.description: Contractual mechanisms (revenue-sharing, fixed-fee-plus-variable-share transfer payments) are used to redistribute government incentives or excess profit fairly between developers and general contractors, achieving supply chain coordination.

codes.label: Equitable allocation of environmental responsibility across supply chain
codes.description: Contractor and supplier tend toward equal splitting of environmental-reduction responsibility/cost under subsidy or reward-penalty mechanisms, suggesting a template for allocating compliance obligations contractually.

categories.label: Labor, Union, and Workforce Considerations in Off-site Logistics
categories.memo: Addresses how labor relations and workforce structures intersect with supply chain and logistics decisions in prefabrication, an aspect distinct from pure materials/module logistics.

codes.label: Union resistance to off-site outsourcing
codes.description: Labor union agreements and resistance to work being moved off-site can constrain or discourage contractors from adopting prefabrication and supply chain outsourcing.

codes.label: Human-robot collaboration and staffing implications
codes.description: Since robots cannot fully replace workers, human-robot collaborative work modes persist, affecting labor allocation, subcontracting complexity, and staffing needs under construction contracts.

codes.label: Phased capacity-building and contractual strategies for adoption
codes.description: Firms are advised to expand prefabrication capability incrementally (outsourcing, small facility, full-scale operation), with attention to evolving contractual and labor portability policies at each stage.

categories.label: Cost Modeling and Economic Trade-offs in Off-site Supply Chains
categories.memo: Covers quantitative/economic modeling of supply chain, transport, and adoption costs that inform contractual and policy decisions, including subsidy design and robotic construction economics.

codes.label: Cost structure differences: robotic vs traditional construction
codes.description: Robotic construction introduces additional cost items (installation/disassembly, freight, maintenance) and stricter material/site requirements not present in traditional construction, requiring new contractual treatment of these costs.

codes.label: Quantified value of optimized logistics/transport planning
codes.description: Formal optimization of JIT transport and module scheduling can reduce total project costs substantially (10-30%) compared to intuitive/rule-of-thumb planning, quantifying the economic case for more rigorous contractual/process specification.

codes.label: Transaction costs borne by developers/owners
codes.description: Developers incur significant transaction costs (estimating, partner identification, approvals, monitoring, negotiation) associated with managing prefabrication supply chains, often underestimated in project cost planning.

codes.label: Bilevel government-contractor cost/subsidy modeling
codes.description: Optimal subsidy policy design requires modeling contractor cost-minimization responses under uncertainty in construction volume, costs, and supply, since ignoring these factors produces suboptimal contractual/policy outcomes.

categories.label: Early Involvement and Upfront Commitment Requirements
categories.memo: Concerns the front-loaded design/planning commitments that off-site logistics require, and how this inflexibility interacts with contractual delivery structures.

codes.label: Early supplier/fabricator involvement in design
codes.description: Prefabrication requires suppliers, manufacturers, or fabricators to be engaged early (sometimes unpaid) in design to prevent unbuildable or overly costly designs, and to align design with logistics/transport constraints.

codes.label: Design freeze and reduced flexibility for later changes
codes.description: Off-site prefabrication requires early design finalization because modules must be manufactured before construction starts, conflicting with the industry's traditional tolerance for late design changes and creating contractual tension.

codes.label: Mock-up/inspection mechanisms for dispute prevention
codes.description: Client-approved mock-up modules and third-party inspections at manufacturing sites are used as contractual risk-avoidance and quality-assurance mechanisms prior to full-scale production.
